prompt: Which of these do BigQuery, Snowflake and Redshift have in common? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Columnar, compressed storage
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Parallel processing on many machines
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Storage kept apart from compute
choices.why: Yes, in all three today.

choices.text: The same way of charging for compute
choices.why: Bytes, seconds and node hours: three different bills.

prompt: What in lessons 2 to 6 changes when the warehouse moves to one of these products?

choices.text: Nothing in the model
choices.why: Right. The bill and the physical knobs change; facts, dimensions and history do not.

choices.text: Type 2 history is no longer needed, because the product keeps versions of every table
choices.why: Table versions are about recovery, not about where a customer lived when they bought.

choices.text: Star schemas must become snowflakes to run in the cloud
choices.why: All three run a star as written.

choices.text: Surrogate keys are replaced by the provider's own identifiers
choices.why: No provider assigns your dimension keys.

prompt: What is a slot in BigQuery?

choices.text: A partition of a table, one per day
choices.why: Partitions are storage; slots are compute.

choices.text: A saved query that runs on a schedule
choices.why: That is a scheduled query.

choices.text: A unit of processing capacity
choices.why: Right. A query gets as many as it can use, up to the project's limit.

choices.text: A column reserved for clustering
choices.why: Clustering columns are ordinary columns.

prompt: Why does the BigQuery version of `fact_sales` use a `DATE` column instead of `date_key`?

choices.text: BigQuery has no integer type
choices.why: It has `INT64`.

choices.text: To partition the table by date
choices.why: Right. `dim_date` stays, joined on the date.

choices.text: Dates compress better than integers in Google's format, saving most of the storage bill
choices.why: Storage is not why; the partition clause is.

choices.text: Surrogate keys are forbidden
choices.why: The other keys stay integers.

prompt: At BigQuery's on-demand price of US$ 6.25 per TiB, what would 4 TiB of queries cost in a month, before the free tebibyte is deducted?
A query reads 3 INT64 columns of a table with 887,477 rows. How many bytes does BigQuery's on-demand model count for that table?
`dim_date` is 11,712 bytes for the query. What is it billed?

choices.text: 11,712 bytes
choices.why: Below the minimum.

choices.text: Nothing, because dimensions are free
choices.why: The price page makes no such exception.

choices.text: 1 TiB, the monthly free tier
choices.why: The free tier is an allowance, not a charge per table.

choices.text: 10 MB, the minimum per table
choices.why: Right. Every table referenced is billed at least 10 MB.

prompt: An analyst adds `LIMIT 10` to a `SELECT *` over a large BigQuery table to keep it cheap. What does the bill do?

choices.text: It drops to ten rows' worth
choices.why: The price counts columns read, not rows shown.

choices.text: It doubles, because the result is sorted
choices.why: There is no sort here.

choices.text: It stays the same: every column is billed whole
choices.why: Right. Name fewer columns, or filter on the partition.

choices.text: It becomes free, under the 10 MB minimum
choices.why: A minimum is a floor, not a ceiling.

prompt: What is a virtual warehouse in Snowflake?

choices.text: A named cluster that runs queries
choices.why: Right. Compute, sized and started apart from the data.

choices.text: A schema that holds a copy of the data for one team
choices.why: Warehouses hold no data; they read the shared tables.

choices.text: A data mart
choices.why: A mart is a set of tables; a virtual warehouse is compute.

choices.text: A view
choices.why: Views are SQL; warehouses are machines.

prompt: Snowflake tables have no partition clause. How are blocks skipped, then?

choices.text: They are never skipped; every query reads every block
choices.why: The statistics exist so they can be.

choices.text: By an index the user creates on each column
choices.why: Snowflake does not ask for indexes on its tables.

choices.text: By hashing the distribution key
choices.why: That is Redshift's question.

choices.text: Micro-partitions with min and max per column
choices.why: Right. A clustering key makes them useful for the columns that matter.

prompt: A Medium Snowflake warehouse (4 credits an hour) runs a query for 90 seconds. How many credits does it consume?
A Large warehouse (8 credits an hour) is resumed for a 3-second query and suspended right after. How many credits is it billed?
hint: There is a minimum each time it resumes. Give three decimals.

prompt: A query parallelises perfectly. Moving it from Small to Medium does what to its cost?
hint: Twice the rate, half the time.

choices.text: Doubles it
choices.why: The time halves too.

choices.text: Leaves it the same
choices.why: Right. In practice Amdahl's law makes it somewhat more.

choices.text: Halves it
choices.why: The rate doubles.

choices.text: Makes it free for the first minute of every hour
choices.why: The first minute is a minimum, not a gift.

prompt: Which habits reduce a Snowflake bill? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Auto-suspend after a short idle period
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Sizing up only for heavy loads
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Queries that read less
choices.why: Yes: they run for less time.

choices.text: Keeping one warehouse running all day for every team
choices.why: It is billed whether busy or not.

prompt: In a provisioned Redshift cluster, what does the leader node do?

choices.text: Plans queries and combines results
choices.why: Right. The compute nodes do the scanning.

choices.text: Stores the largest table
choices.why: Tables are spread over compute nodes.

choices.text: Backs up the other nodes
choices.why: Backups are a separate service.

choices.text: Runs only the dashboards
choices.why: Every query goes through it.

prompt: Match each Redshift distribution style to what it suits.

pairs.right: Large tables joined on one column
Small dimensions copied to every node
Tables with no good key and no joins

prompt: Why `DISTKEY (order_id)` and not `DISTKEY (shop_key)` for Ana's fact table?

choices.text: Shop keys are text, and a distribution key has to be an integer column
choices.why: Both are integers, and text keys are allowed.

choices.text: Order numbers sort the table by date
choices.why: Sorting is the SORTKEY's job.

choices.text: Seven shops put 72% of rows on one node
choices.why: Right. Order numbers spread four nodes within half a per cent.

choices.text: Redshift forbids distributing by a dimension key
choices.why: It allows it; it would just be skewed here.

prompt: The Redshift clause that stores a table's rows in date order, so zone maps can skip blocks, is ___ (date_key).
Which declaration in each product aims at keeping together the rows a query wants?

choices.text: Slots; credits; RPUs
choices.why: Those are units of compute and billing.

choices.text: Partitions and clusters; clustering keys; sort keys
choices.why: Right. BigQuery, Snowflake and Redshift, in that order.

choices.text: Datasets; databases; schemas
choices.why: Those are containers of tables.

choices.text: `DISTKEY` in all three
choices.why: Only Redshift has it, and it is about machines, not blocks.

prompt: A team designs its tables around one product's knobs, putting billing tricks into the model. What risk does the lesson point to?

choices.text: The product refuses to run star schemas
choices.why: All three run them.

choices.text: Queries become slower than on PostgreSQL
choices.why: Nothing suggests that.

choices.text: History can no longer be kept
choices.why: History is a modelling choice any product supports.

choices.text: The model cannot move with only its DDL rewritten
choices.why: Right. A dimensional model moves; one built on knobs does not.

prompt: Which product in this list runs in a single process on one machine and is the engine of this course?
hint: Every query in the course ran on it.

choices.text: ClickHouse
choices.why: A columnar server, not this course's engine.

choices.text: Databricks SQL
choices.why: A managed service over Delta Lake.

choices.text: DuckDB
choices.why: Right. MotherDuck is a managed service built around it.

choices.text: Microsoft Fabric
choices.why: Microsoft's warehouse and lake product.

prompt: Put the lesson's questions for choosing a warehouse in the order it gives them.
items: How much operation does the team want?
What does the rest of the stack speak?
trap: Starting from benchmarks is the slip the section warns about: at most companies' size every product answers in seconds.

prompt: Ponto Final's warehouse is a 46 MB file. What does the lesson say about renting a cloud warehouse for it now?

choices.text: Not yet; one machine is the simpler answer
choices.why: Right. The model will move when it is worth it.

choices.text: It is required once there are two tables
choices.why: Nothing requires it.

choices.text: BigQuery, because its free tier covers it, and that settles the question for good
choices.why: Cheap today is not the same as needed.

choices.text: Redshift, because shops use AWS
choices.why: Nothing says where Ponto Final's data lives.

prompt: Dashboards refresh every five minutes against a 2 TiB fact table, reading 4 of its 40 columns, filtered to the last week on a date-partitioned table. Under BigQuery on demand, which change cuts the bill most?
hint: Bytes read per refresh, times refreshes.

choices.text: Adding `LIMIT 100` to each query
choices.why: LIMIT does not reduce bytes read.

choices.text: Moving to `SELECT *` so the cache is shared
choices.why: That bills all 40 columns.

choices.text: Removing the date partition
choices.why: Then every refresh reads the whole history.

choices.text: Refreshing from a small aggregate rebuilt after each load
choices.why: Right. The dashboards read kilobytes instead of a week of four columns, every five minutes.
